description: VIKKI STAR is participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. My challenge is to explore equipment left behind on Moon and Mars through creative story telling. I am interested in Space Science.
summary: The ‘VIKKI STAR’ team is participating in the ‘NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026’. Team Members: SREERAM S. For this challenge, I have chosen the challenge: “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.” As part of this, I have crafted a story centered on the equipment left behind by NASA on Mars (the Red Planet) during the 'Viking' mission. The characters include Rohan, an eleven-year-old member of a space club; his teacher; his mother; and two spacecraft named 'Vikki' and 'Viktu'. NASA's Viking 1 and Viking 2 missions are discussed in detail—covering their components, launch dates, objectives, how they successfully achieved their goals, and their current status. Also examined whether the spacecraft could be made operational again and suggested potential solutions to be kept in mind in future. Since the protagonist is a school student, the narrative is presented from his perspective.
details:
I have prepared a story about the equipment that NASA left behind on Mars (the Red Planet) as part of the Viking mission.

•   Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, and the seventh largest. Mars is one of the most explored bodies in our solar system, and it’s the only planet where we’ve sent rovers to explore the alien landscape.

•  NASA's Viking 1 and Viking 2 missions—which each consisted of an orbiter and a lander—represent one of the greatest leaps in planetary exploration history.

•  Two identical space probes were sent to Mars in 1975 to map the planet, study its atmosphere and surface and search for signs and life.

•  Their components, objectives, and how they successfully achieved their goals were explained in detail.

. The craft eventually failed, one by one, as follows:-

VIKING 2 ORBITER

Arrival Date              : August 7, 1976

Shut-off Date            : July 25, 1978

Operational life time : 1 year, 11 months, 18 days

Causes of failure       : Shut down after fuel leak in propulsion system

VIKING 2 LANDER

Arrival Date              : September 3, 1976

Shut-off Date            : April 11, 1980

Operational life time : 3 years, 7months, 8 days

Causes of failure       : Battery failure

VIKING 1 ORBITER

Arrival Date              : June 19, 1976

Shut-off Date            : August 17, 1980

Operational life time : 4 years, 1 month, 19 days

Causes of failure       : Shut down after depletion of altitude control fuel

VIKING 1 LANDER

Arrival Date              : July 20, 1976

Shut-off Date            : November 13, 1982

Operational life time : 6 years, 3 months, 22 days

Causes of failure      : Human error during software update caused the lander’s antenna                                 to go down, terminating communication.

•   All four major components of the NASA Viking program—the Viking 1 Orbiter & Lander and the Viking 2 Orbiter & Lander—were left abandoned (shut down) in space or on the surface of Mars after their missions ended.

•  Is it possible to reactivate spacecraft was analyzed and found that the abandoned Viking 1 and Viking 2 spacecraft cannot return to Earth. They are permanently stuck on Mars and in its orbit due to physics, a lack of fuel, and the degradation of their components.

•  When NASA built and launched them in the 1970s, the necessary technology, fuel capacity, and infrastructure to bring a spacecraft back from the surface of another planet did not exist.

•   The only way a Viking spacecraft will ever return to Earth is if a future human mission physically recovers them, packs them onto a heavy-lift return rocket, and flies them back to Earth as museum artefacts.

•   What lies in the dust is not merely a rusted machine part, but rather a continuation of human curiosity. To those who know how to observe closely, it continues to speak to us even today.

•   Every major leap in space exploration began as an engineering problem that seemed impossible to overcome. The unknown is merely a boundary—until a bridge is built to cross it.

•  Our Mars exploration project should not be limited merely to overcoming existing technical constraints; rather, its goal must be to provide future explorers with the tools they need to look toward the next horizon and say, "Let us go there."

•   We must not only make preparations for an upcoming mission; we should also engage in activities that satisfy the curiosity driving us forward.

•   'Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog' (CHAPEA) is a series of missions conducted by NASA that simulate living on the surface of Mars for a duration of about one year.

•  Two CHAPEA missions have been successfully completed. With the completion of the third mission, it will be possible to land humans on Mars. Let us wait for that day.....
